title: History of paint
titleCn: 颜料的历史：从史前洞穴到古埃及

paragraphs.text: Morning, everyone. Today, we're looking at the history of paint. As you're about to see, there's a lot to be said about it. So today, I'm just going to focus on ancient techniques for producing paint. We'll deal with prehistoric times to about the end of the Roman Empire.

So let's start with the prehistoric era. As I'm sure you're all aware, it's impossible to determine exactly when colors were first used by humans in art. But what we do know is what those first colors were made of and how they were applied.

Researchers have determined that the first colors came from clay, which was most likely used to create marks on the face. Of course, the art from this paint, as we'll call it, wasn't permanent, so it's difficult for us to know much more about what it was used for or who used it.

However, some evidence of ancient paint has been found in Australia. There, scientists have discovered early forms of paint in drawings inside caves. Of course, as you'd expect, the colors used in these drawings are simple, earthy colors, and people would have had to make them from naturally occurring materials around them, such as charcoal from their fires.

One of the problems with the ancient paint was that it didn't last long. It was only temporary because it faded easily or got blown away by the wind or washed off in rain. It wasn't until people introduced other elements, such as animal fats, to the paint, that this problem was solved. In studying this ancient paint, scientists have determined that another popular additive, something that you wouldn't have expected at all, was honey.
Surprising perhaps, but there you go. It worked well enough for us to be able to enjoy their artwork today.

With the advent of more permanent colors, paints could be transported long distances. This is important because there is evidence to suggest that colors were valuable and may have been used at one time or another as a type of money in some of these early societies.

The next important stage in paint history was in the time of the ancient Egyptian Empire. With wealth and power, monuments were constructed and decorated, and also a large number of temples. This led to the development of a wider range of paint.

Interestingly, we now know that one of the problems with much of the paint used at that time, and actually for centuries after, was that it was toxic, though it is unlikely that the artists of the time were aware of that.
The Egyptian era saw the introduction of many new colors. Egyptian blue is one of the best-known colors of that time. It is thought to be the first paint color made by man.

It is not a color that exists in nature. Craftsmen of the time had perfected the art of making this unusual dark blue color, and it's a color that historians strongly identify with Egyptian culture at this time. The color Egyptian blue was produced by crushing up blue glass very finely. This color was very popular in Egypt, and it was common for the wealthy to use it as decoration on their tombs.
Red earth, another paint color that emerged at that time, was also created by a crushing process. This color was produced when minerals that were red in color were ground into a very fine powder.

The Roman Empire also contributed a lot to the expanding range of paint colors available to artists. They extracted all sorts of colors from a wide variety of plants. But perhaps the most interesting color of Roman times was the paint pigment called dragon's blood. As its name suggests, it was a red-colored pigment. It was incredibly popular at the time, most likely due to the belief that the paint was a mixture of the blood from fights between dragons, which people really believed in then, and elephants. At the time, the idea of dragons was very exotic and exciting, and the color was much sought after. However, of course, the paint color was not actually from any animal at all. It came from the tree trunks of a species of tree from Southeast Asia, or more specifically, the gum from the trunks of those trees. Not nearly as exciting as dragons, sadly. Now we'll start looking at...
That is the end of section four.
